title: Scaling Categorical Flow Maps

paper.title: Scaling Categorical Flow Maps
paper.abstract: Abstract Continuous diffusion and flow matching models could represent a powerful alternative to autoregressive approaches for language modelling (LM), as they unlock a host of advantages currently reserved for continuous modalities, including accelerated sampling and tilting. Recently, several works have demonstrated the possibility of generating discrete data continuously by a simple flow matching process between a Gaussian and the one-hot encoded data distribution. They have further shown the feasibility of accelerated sampling via Categorical Flow Maps (CFMs), resulting in competitive sample quality in the few-step regime. However, this method had only been evaluated at relatively modest scales ( < 1 <1 B), leaving the question of its scalability completely open. In this article, we train a 1.7 1.7 B-parameter base flow model on 2.1 2.1 T tokens and self-distill it into a CFM that generates diverse, high-quality text in as few as 4 4 inference steps while maintaining near-data-level token entropy. Furthermore, we introduce a likelihood bound for CFMs in the semi-discrete setting, and show that they can be used to score the model on standard LM benchmarks, achieving results in the same range as discrete diffusion methods. Finally, we uncover some of the challenges that arise from training these models at scale, and we provide prescriptive insights on loss weighting and time scheduling.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Although in language modelling the dominant paradigm has remained autoregressive (AR), diffusion models ( Sohl-Dickstein et al., 2015 ; Ho et al., 2020 ) and flow matching ( Lipman et al., 2023 ; Albergo et al., 2023 ) were responsible for large breakthroughs on continuous modalities. Driven by their success, a line of work has sought to extend diffusion to discrete distributions, an approach coined discrete diffusion ( Austin et al., 2021 ; Hoogeboom et al., 2021 ; Campbell et al., 2022 ; Sahoo et al., 2024 ; Shi et al., 2024 ; Gat et al., 2024 ) . The hope of these models was to extend the rich and principled diffusion toolbox to discrete data, including guidance ( Ho and Salimans, 2022 ) , distribution tilting ( Domingo-Enrich et al., 2025 ) , and accelerated sampling ( Song et al., 2023 ; Song and Dhariwal, 2023 ) . However, discrete diffusion methods evolve on the discrete grid, preventing the usage of the well-established continuous techniques. Figure 1 : (Left) Gen PPL vs. NFE. (Right) Token entropy vs. NFE. The gray band indicates the token entropy of the data distribution. Above the circled points are provided short qualitative samples that reflect the generation quality at that NFE regime. Self-distillation enables high-quality, diverse generation at significantly fewer function evaluations. A parallel line of work developed continuous-state processes to generate discrete data, either on the simplex ( Stark et al., 2024 ; Davis et al., 2024 ; Cheng et al., 2024 ) or directly in ℝ d \mathbb{R}^{d} ( Eijkelboom et al., 2025 ) . Recently, Roos et al. (2026) ; Lee et al. (2026) ; Potaptchik et al. (2026b) scaled these ideas to common discrete diffusion benchmarks, and showed that these methods are competitive, but also succeeded in porting flow map matching ( Boffi et al., 2025a ; Boffi et al., 2025b ) to discrete data, enabling high quality few-step sampling. We refer to these methods as Categorical Flow Maps (CFMs). If successful at scale, CFMs could unlock the flow map toolbox for steering and fine-tuning ( Holderrieth et al., 2026 ; Potaptchik et al., 2026a ) , trading compute for sample quality rather than merely generating plausible outputs. Nonetheless, it remains unclear whether CFMs can scale to the billion-parameter, trillion-token regime. For a token vocabulary V V , and context length L L , they require materialising L × | V | L\times\lvert V\rvert logit matrices, where | V | \lvert V\rvert can easily attain 200,000 200{,}000 tokens in modern LLMs, imposing a significant memory and computational overhead. In this work, we show that CFMs scale competitively to this setting. Our contributions are as follows: • We explore the CFM design space via 350 350 + configurations at 400 400 M proxy scale, identifying robust hyperparameter settings that inform the full-scale run ( Section 3 ). • We train a 1.7 1.7 B-parameter flow matching model on 2.1 2.1 T tokens, directly comparing to masked and uniform diffusion ( Sahoo et al., 2026a ) under matched compute ( Section 4 ). • We self-distill the pretrained flow into a CFM, improving the quality vs. NFE Pareto front in the few-step regime ( Figure 1 ). • To enable likelihood-based evaluation, we provide a semi-discrete ELBO, and report results on MCQA benchmarks in similar ranges as other non-autoregressive methods ( Section 4.3 ). While we uncover some of the limitations of the method as well, we demonstrate the viability of CFMs at this scale.

sections.heading: 2.1 Autoregressive Modelling
sections.text: AR models approach language modelling by decomposing the joint distribution over a sequence into a product of conditional distributions using the chain rule of probability: p data ( x 1 : L ) = ∏ i = 1 L p ( x i ∣ x < i ) , p_{\mathrm{data}}(x_{1:L})=\prod_{i=1}^{L}p(x_{i}\mid x_{<i}), (2.1) where x < i = ( x 1 , … , x i − 1 ) x_{<i}=(x_{1},\dots,x_{i-1}) denotes the prefix preceding token x i x_{i} . This factorisation converts the problem of modelling a sequence into a next-token prediction problem. A parametric model p θ p_{\theta} is trained to approximate these conditional distributions by maximising the likelihood of observed sequences in the training corpus.

sections.heading: 3 Pretraining a flow
sections.text: Figure 3 : Mixture schedules for varying λ ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] \lambda\in[0,1] at vocabulary size 100 100 k. Current best-performing approaches for CFMs rely on a two-stage training ( Lee et al., 2026 ; Potaptchik et al., 2026b ) : in the first stage, a simple cross-entropy denoiser is trained (see equation 2.10 ); in the second stage, that denoiser is self-distilled into a CFM (see equations 2.12 and 2.11 ). The two-stage approach is necessary, because the self-distillation objectives rely on a biased signal from the model itself, so applying them from the start degrades final performance. Moreover, self-distillation objectives are computationally demanding (requiring multiple forward passes per gradient step), making their optimisation over the entire training trajectory prohibitively expensive. In this section, we investigate the importance of three components in the design space of CFM pretraining: the time schedule mixture, the adaptive loss weight, and the random “unmasking” of inputs. Finally, we sweep over optimiser hyperparameters, and discuss the possibility of their transfer to larger scales.

sections.heading: Time scheduling.
sections.text: Lee et al. (2026) ; Potaptchik et al. (2026b) show the importance of the time schedule for CFMs. Instead of the linear interpolant schedule, a monotone map γ : [ 0 , 1 ] → [ 0 , 1 ] \gamma:[0,1]\to[0,1] , coined the “error decoding” schedule ( Sahoo et al., 2025 ; Pynadath et al., 2025 ) , significantly improves the final model’s performance. This schedule adapts the time so that the probability of incorrectly decoding the current point, P ⁡ ( argmax I t ≠ argmax I 1 ) P(\mathop{\mathrm{argmax}}I_{t}\neq\mathop{\mathrm{argmax}}I_{1}) , grows linearly in t t , instead of exhibiting a sharp phase transition of the linear schedule. They report that a convex combination of it with the linear schedule, α t = ( 1 − λ ) ​ t + λ ​ γ t \alpha_{t}=(1-\lambda)t+\lambda\gamma_{t} , further improves the generation quality. While Potaptchik et al. (2026b) train with λ = 0.9 \lambda=0.9 , Lee et al. (2026) use it only at inference with λ ∈ { 0.5 , 0.75 , 1 } \lambda\in\{0.5,0.75,1\} . We ablate over this mixture choice.

sections.text: Potaptchik et al. (2026b) adopt the adaptive loss weight of Geng et al. The resulting objective is ℒ w ​ ( θ ) = 𝔼 x ​ [ w ⁡ ( x ) ​ KL ⁡ ( p ∥ q ) ] . \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{w}}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{x}\Big[w(x)\operatorname{KL}\!\left(p\,\middle\|\,q\right)\Big]. (3.1) This upweights low-error regions and downweights high-error ones in order to stabilise training. We also assess the importance of this weight.

sections.heading: Random unmasking of input sequence
sections.text: The models are by default only trained on generating full, unconditional sequences, but final downstream applications typically require conditional generation given prompts. To match this setting, we follow Dieleman et al. (2022) , and with a probability p p unmask a random prefix of the text, sampled from 𝒰 ⁡ [ 1 , L / d ] \mathcal{U}[1,L/d] , with d | L d\mid L . We vary both p p and d d .

sections.heading: Setup.
sections.text: We train a 400 400 M-parameter adaptation of diffusion transformers from SEDD ( Lou et al., 2023 ) , which is also used in Roos et al. (2026) ; Lee et al. (2026) . In particular, we use the transformer from Roos et al. (2026) , which follow the recommendations of Zhou et al. (2025) to upper-bound the Lipschitz constant of the model for more stable training. We train over 16 16 B tokens, resulting in about 40 40 tokens per parameter over the Nemotron pre-training dataset ( Basant et al., 2025 ) using the TikToken tokenizer ( OpenAI, 2023 ) . As in Nie et al. (2025) , we also randomly crop sequences to ensure the models have been trained on different context lengths. We sweep over the mixture schedule λ ∈ [ 0 , 0.25 , 0.5 , 0.75 , 1 ] \lambda\in[0,0.25,0.5,0.75,1] , adaptive loss weight on ( r = 0.5 r=0.5 ) and off ( r = 0 r=0 ), and the clean prefix probability p ∈ [ 0 , 0.25 , 0.5 ] p\in[0,0.25,0.5] .

sections.heading: Metrics.
sections.text: We evaluate our models using generative perplexity (Gen PPL, ↓ \downarrow ) and MAUVE ⋆ \star ( ↑ \uparrow ) ( Pillutla et al., 2021 ) over 128 128 inference steps. For Gen PPL, we use Qwen 2.5 7 7 B ( Yang et al., 2025 ) to compute the perplexity of unconditionally generated samples from our models with L = 1024 L=1024 , measuring general sample quality. For MAUVE ⋆ \star , we extract sequences of length L = 512 L=512 from Nemotron, drop their second half, and use our model to generate the completion. Embeddings computed on both the original samples and the generated samples with GPT-2 ( Radford et al., 2019 ) are used to measure similarity. A score of 1.0 1.0 indicates completions indistinguishable from the original ones on the distributional level, measuring prompt completion quality and diversity.

sections.heading: Results.
sections.text: Figure 4 summarises our first sweep over a total of 30 30 configurations. Adaptive loss weighting ( r = 0.5 r=0.5 ) uniformly improves Gen PPL but slightly degrades MAUVE ⋆ \star , revealing a trade-off between token-level quality and distributional fidelity. Since MAUVE ⋆ \star is upper-bounded by 1 1 , the Gen PPL gain is more practically meaningful than the MAUVE ⋆ \star degradation at these values. We confirm this in Section 4 , where MAUVE ⋆ \star reaches near-maximal values (about 0.94 0.94 ) despite having the adaptive loss weight enabled. The schedule optimum lies near λ = 0.75 \lambda=0.75 , with a sharp collapse at λ = 1 \lambda=1 , which shows that pure error-decoding without mixing is detrimental. Clean prefix probability p > 0 p>0 is essential for MAUVE ⋆ \star : without it, scores remain near zero regardless of other settings, resulting in out-of-distribution outputs. In a follow-up grid of 324 324 configurations ( Figure 5 ), we narrow the ranges around these best settings and find that Gen PPL and MAUVE ⋆ \star are primarily sensitive to learning rate and weight decay, while p p , d d , and λ \lambda are robust in the selected range. Figure 5 : Marginal effect of each swept hyperparameter on Gen PPL (top) and MAUVE ⋆ \star (bottom), averaged over all other variables ( 324 324 configurations). Shaded regions denote ± 1 \pm 1 standard deviation. Learning rate and weight decay are the primary drivers; p p , d d , and λ \lambda are robust in the narrowed range.

sections.heading: 3.3 Hyperparameter transfer
sections.text: Searching for optimal hyperparameters directly at large scale is expensive. Therefore, it is common to rely on zero-shot hyperparameter transfer rules to identify optimal hyperparameters when scaling the model size, batch size, and token horizon ( Yang et al., 2022 ; Dey et al., 2026 ; Mlodozeniec et al., 2025 ) . We attempted to leverage Complete(d)P ( Mlodozeniec et al., 2025 ) by performing a hyperparameter sweep on a 400 400 M model; see Section D.3 . Since our architecture includes time-conditioning layers that are not covered by existing transfer theories, we adapted the method by treating these layers as hidden layers. However, our experiments in Section D.4 show that the baseline approach, with neither depth nor width transfer, achieved the best performance. We therefore leave zero-shot hyperparameter transfer for CFMs as an open question.

sections.heading: 4 Experiments
sections.text: For the full-scale pretraining experiment, we closely follow the setup of Sahoo et al. (2026a) : we train a 1.7 1.7 B-parameter CFM on the Nemotron Pretraining dataset ( Basant et al., 2025 ) using the TikToken tokenizer ( OpenAI, 2023 ) ( | V | ≈ 100 ​ k |V|\approx 100\text{k} ), with a context length of 2048 2048 tokens. We train on 2.1 2.1 T tokens using 256 256 H100s with a batch size of 10 10 per GPU. We use the architecture of Section D.2 . For the self-distillation phase, we train the models for 200 200 k steps with 64 64 H100s and a batch size of 6 6 , for both PSD and ESD losses. 1 1 1 For the self-distillation round, the number of optimisation steps is more relevant than the number of tokens. For the ESD loss, note that we use finite differences to estimate the derivatives, as using Jacobian-Vector Products (JVPs) on such large models is prohibitively expensive in both memory and time. We find this approach computationally more efficient than the usage of custom kernels ( Zhou et al., 2025 ; Roos et al., 2026 ) . Additionally, we train an autoregressive baseline at the same scale for comparison.

sections.heading: 4.1 1.7B flow pre-training
sections.text: We present our results in Figures 1 and 9 as the “Undistilled” lines. At high inference steps, the flow model reaches Gen PPL competitive with the AR baseline: at 1024 1024 steps, our model attains 58.66 58.66 Gen PPL, vs. 45.33 45.33 for the AR model. As for the MAUVE ⋆ \star score, the model reaches near maximal values at high inference steps (approximately 0.94 0.94 ), and, already at 8 8 steps, exceeds the AR baseline: 0.88 0.88 (ours) vs. 0.7 0.7 (AR). In Section D.5 , we provide additional details on the training dynamics of the model, where we can see that the generation quality steadily improves. Furthermore, we also provide qualitative samples from the undistilled model in Appendix E .

sections.heading: 4.2.1 Design space of self-distillation
sections.text: Figure 6 : Ablation on PSD self-distillation, 10 10 k steps: marginal effect of the divergence on MAUVE ⋆ \star and Gen PPL, averaged over the time-sampling distribution. Figure 7 : Ablation on PSD self-distillation, 10 10 k steps: marginal effect of the ( s , t ) (s,t) time-sampling distribution on MAUVE ⋆ \star and Gen PPL, averaged over the divergence without the reverse KL data. We now investigate how to self-distill the pretrained flow into a CFM. The design space is large, and we explore two axes on short 10 10 k step runs. The first one is the joint time distribution of ( s , t ) (s,t) : we consider the gap-schedule used in Lee et al. (2026) , starting from 10 − 2 10^{-2} and doubling every 500 500 steps (denoted 𝒰 \mathcal{U} ), and the gap logit-normal distribution of Zhou et al. (2025) (denoted ℒ ​ 𝒩 \mathcal{LN} ). As pointed out by Potaptchik et al. (2026b) , we can choose any type of divergence D D for the SD objectives. This constitutes the second axis, as we try the following divergences: forward KL (the default choice, denoted KL \mathrm{KL} ), reverse KL ( RKL \mathrm{RKL} ) and the Jensen-Shannon Divergence ( JSD \mathrm{JSD} ). The optimisation dynamics are discussed in Section D.6.1 : the forward KL reinforces positions on which the teacher and the student concur; in contrast, JSD does not exhibit this behaviour. Avoiding this reinforcement could be preferable, as the teacher is biased and imperfect, and could thus alter the underlying flow. We track Gen PPL and MAUVE ⋆ \star for 1 1 , 2 2 , 4 4 and 128 128 inference steps to observe the effect on few-step generation, and to ensure that the larger step regime remains stable. We report our results in Figure 6 and Figure 7 for PSD. We omit ESD results as all runs diverged; for thoroughness, they are available in Figures 16 and 17 . ESD at this scale exhibited either mode collapse or degraded MAUVE ⋆ \star relative to the undistilled flow, which we attribute to high-variance Jacobian estimates from finite differences. Therefore, we focus on PSD. All self-distillation objectives, except those based on RKL, improve the token entropy of single- and few-step generation, which is also reflected in higher MAUVE ⋆ \star at 4 4 NFE. The uniform distribution produces better entropy at a single step, and better overall quality for NFE ≥ 2 \geq 2 . With the logit-normal distribution, single-step samples have lower entropy, which explains the lower Gen PPL. Based on these findings, we select PSD with both forward KL and JSD divergences, using the uniform time distribution, for the full 200 200 k-step distillation.

sections.heading: 4.2.2 Full self-distillation
sections.text: Figure 8 : MAUVE* vs. NFE. A significant gap between the distilled and undistilled models in the low NFE regime is observable. Figure 9 : Δ \Delta PPL (conditional generation) vs. NFE. The undistilled model produces collapsed outputs for 1 1 NFE. The results of the full-scale, 200 200 k steps self-distillation are available in Figure 1 and Figure 9 . Both flow-maps provide samples substantially closer to the data distribution in terms of token entropy. Moreover, while the undistilled model produced degenerate samples in the 1 1 – 2 2 step regime, which artificially lowers the Gen PPL, the flow map models generate diverse samples, though Gen PPL remains high. The MAUVE ⋆ \star is improved by both models in the few-step regime, with the most prominent improvement at 4 4 sampling steps. The JSD overall seems to slightly degrade generation quality; we hypothesise this is due to the higher token entropy it produces compared to forward KL. We additionally report Delta Perplexity ( Δ \Delta PPL), which measures a model’s ability to complete text conditioned on a dataset prompt. Given a prompt from the dataset, the evaluated model generates the remaining text, and we report the perplexity of the generated completion under Qwen 2.5 7B ( Yang et al., 2025 ) . Depicted in Figure 9 , the Δ \Delta PPL of the self-distilled models improves significantly in the few-step regime, while recovering similar perplexities for more inference steps.

sections.heading: Semi-discrete ELBO.
sections.text: Standard LM benchmarks require scoring answer choices by likelihood, which is not directly available from a flow-based model. sections.heading: Continuous diffusion for discrete data.
sections.text: Early work by Dieleman et al. (2022) attempted to learn the embeddings of the discrete data using the reparametrisation trick; Li et al. (2022) explored a similar approach with word embeddings. Later, Stark et al. (2024) designed an interpolation scheme directly on the simplex. Davis et al. (2024) ; Cheng et al. (2024) leveraged Riemannian geometry to alleviate the issues of linear interpolants. Variational Flow Matching ( Eijkelboom et al., 2025 ) shows how to flow from a Gaussian to one-hot encoded data. CFM ( Roos et al., 2026 ) , FMLM ( Lee et al., 2026 ) , and DFM ( Potaptchik et al., 2026b ) adopted this approach, and reached competitive performance with discrete diffusion baselines. Our work builds directly on this line, and demonstrates its scalability to the 1.7 1.7 B parameter regime.

sections.heading: Accelerated sampling.
sections.text: Consistency models ( Song et al., 2023 ; Song and Dhariwal, 2023 ) pioneered the idea of mapping any point along a diffusion trajectory to the trajectory’s endpoint, enabling one- or few-step generation. Flow map matching ( Boffi et al., 2025a ; Boffi et al., 2025b ; Geng et al., 2025 ) provides a principled framework for learning such maps via self-distillation of a pretrained flow. CFMs ( Roos et al., 2026 ; Lee et al., 2026 ; Potaptchik et al., 2026b ) port flow map matching to the semi-discrete setting, reducing inference to a single forward pass while retaining the continuous-state benefits. Other related works are discussed in Appendix A .

sections.heading: 6 Limitations
sections.text: CFMs require materialising full L × | V | L\times\lvert V\rvert continuous-state trajectory matrices for all steps. At our scale ( L = 2048 L=2048 , | V | ≈ 100 ​ k \lvert V\rvert\approx 100\text{k} ), this is manageable given sufficient hardware ( 256 256 H100s), but the cost grows linearly in context length and vocabulary size. We absorb this bottleneck through compute and efficient cross-entropy implementation ( Wijmans et al., 2025 ) , without solving it. Moreover, CFMs also present challenges in principled hyperparameter transfer. Unlike standard transformers, CFMs condition on continuous times via dedicated layers, which fall outside the parametrisations covered by Complete(d)P ( Mlodozeniec et al., 2025 ) . Our attempts to apply Complete(d)P to this architecture resulted in worse performance than direct tuning at the target scale. Adapting time-conditioned variants of μ \mu P ( Zheng et al., 2025 ) is left for future work.

sections.heading: 7 Conclusion
sections.text: We have shown that Categorical Flow Maps scale competitively to the 1.7 1.7 B-parameter regime. After self-distillation, they produce diverse, high-quality text in as few as 4 4 function evaluations while maintaining near-data-level token entropy, pushing the quality vs. throughput Pareto front beyond discrete diffusion baselines. Our semi-discrete ELBO places the model in the same ballpark as other non-autoregressive methods, though a gap remains with approaches trained directly on ELBO maximisation. These results suggest that continuous-state generation is a viable path for discrete data at LLM scale, and that the broader flow map toolbox (guidance, tilting, reward fine-tuning) is now within reach for language modelling.

sections.heading: Continuous diffusion for discrete data.
sections.text: With a different approach, Chen et al. (2026) proposed a way of learning continuous trajectories for discrete data, leveraging embedding spaces and Bregman divergences.

sections.heading: Discrete diffusion.
sections.text: Diffusion models for discrete state spaces originate from D3PM ( Austin et al., 2021 ) and multinomial diffusion ( Hoogeboom et al., 2021 ) , which design discrete forward processes whose reversal can be learned by a neural network. Campbell et al. (2022) recast the framework in continuous time and consider the rate transition matrices of the reverse CTMC. SEDD ( Lou et al., 2023 ) replaces the standard ELBO with a score-entropy objective, improving both training stability and sample quality. Masked diffusion ( Sahoo et al., 2024 ; Shi et al., 2024 ) simplified the earlier approaches, resulting in a simple cross-entropy objective that forms an ELBO on the data distribution. Discrete Flow Matching ( Gat et al., 2024 ) generalised the framework by learning a probability velocity field over discrete states. ( Schiff et al., 2024 ) further investigated the uniform-state case of discrete diffusion.

sections.heading: Accelerated sampling for discrete diffusion.
sections.text: Several approaches have attempted to implement accelerated methods for discrete diffusion. Sahoo et al. (2025) shows how a continuous Gaussian latent can generate a uniform-state discrete diffusion process, enabling consistent trajectories for SDTT-like self-distillation ( Deschenaux and Gulcehre, 2025 ) . Hayakawa et al. (2025) show that by incorporating correlation through diffusion steps the few-step sampling regime can be improved. Based on similar observations, Yoo et al. (2025) propose to refine the couplings between source and target distributions.

In this article, we train a 1.7 1.7 B-parameter base flow model on 2.1 2.1 T tokens and self-distill it into a CFM that generates diverse, high-quality text in as few as 4 4 inference steps while maintaining near-data-level token entropy. Work done during an internship at Apple. 1 Introduction Although in language modelling the dominant paradigm has remained autoregressive (AR), diffusion models ( Sohl-Dickstein et al., 2015 ; Ho et al., 2020 ) and flow matching ( Lipman et al., 2023 ; Albergo et al., 2023 ) were responsible for large breakthroughs on continuous modalities. Driven by their success, a line of work has sought to extend diffusion to discrete distributions, an approach coined discrete diffusion ( Austin et al., 2021 ; Hoogeboom et al., 2021 ; Campbell et al., 2022 ; Sahoo et al., 2024 ; Shi et al., 2024 ; Gat et al., 2024 ) . The hope of these models was to extend the rich and principled diffusion toolbox to discrete data, including guidance ( Ho and Salimans, 2022 ) , distribution tilting ( Domingo-Enrich et al., 2025 ) , and accelerated sampling ( Song et al., 2023 ; Song and Dhariwal, 2023 ) . However, discrete diffusion methods evolve on the discrete grid, preventing the usage of the well-established continuous techniques. Figure 1 : (Left) Gen PPL vs. NFE. (Right) Token entropy vs. NFE. The gray band indicates the token entropy of the data distribution. Above the circled points are provided short qualitative samples that reflect the generation quality at that NFE regime. Self-distillation enables high-quality, diverse generation at significantly fewer function evaluations. A parallel line of work developed continuous-state processes to generate discrete data, either on the simplex ( Stark et al., 2024 ; Davis et al., 2024 ; Cheng et al., 2024 ) or directly in ℝ d \mathbb{R}^{d} ( Eijkelboom et al., 2025 ) . Recently, Roos et al. (2026) ; Lee et al. (2026) ; Potaptchik et al. (2026b) scaled these ideas to common discrete diffusion benchmarks, and showed that these methods are competitive, but also succeeded in porting flow map matching ( Boffi et al., 2025a ; Boffi et al., 2025b ) to discrete data, enabling high quality few-step sampling. We refer to these methods as Categorical Flow Maps (CFMs). If successful at scale, CFMs could unlock the flow map toolbox for steering and fine-tuning ( Holderrieth et al., 2026 ; Potaptchik et al., 2026a ) , trading compute for sample quality rather than merely generating plausible outputs. Nonetheless, it remains unclear whether CFMs can scale to the billion-parameter, trillion-token regime. For a token vocabulary V V , and context length L L , they require materialising L × | V | L\times\lvert V\rvert logit matrices, where | V | \lvert V\rvert can easily attain 200,000 200{,}000 tokens in modern LLMs, imposing a significant memory and computational overhead. In this work, we show that CFMs scale competitively to this setting. Our contributions are as follows: • We explore the CFM design space via 350 350 + configurations at 400 400 M proxy scale, identifying robust hyperparameter settings that inform the full-scale run ( Section 3 ). • We train a 1.7 1.7 B-parameter flow matching model on 2.1 2.1 T tokens, directly comparing to masked and uniform diffusion ( Sahoo et al., 2026a ) under matched compute ( Section 4 ). • We self-distill the pretrained flow into a CFM, improving the quality vs. NFE Pareto front in the few-step regime ( Figure 1 ). • To enable likelihood-based evaluation, we provide a semi-discrete ELBO, and report results on MCQA benchmarks in similar ranges as other non-autoregressive methods ( Section 4.3 ). Current best-performing approaches for CFMs rely on a two-stage training ( Lee et al., 2026 ; Potaptchik et al., 2026b ) : in the first stage, a simple cross-entropy denoiser is trained (see equation 2.10 ); in the second stage, that denoiser is self-distilled into a CFM (see equations 2.12 and 2.11 ). The two-stage approach is necessary, because the self-distillation objectives rely on a biased signal from the model itself, so applying them from the start degrades final performance. Moreover, self-distillation objectives are computationally demanding (requiring multiple forward passes per gradient step), making their optimisation over the entire training trajectory prohibitively expensive. In this section, we investigate the importance of three components in the design space of CFM pretraining: the time schedule mixture, the adaptive loss weight, and the random “unmasking” of inputs. Finally, we sweep over optimiser hyperparameters, and discuss the possibility of their transfer to larger scales. 3.1 Design space of CFMs Time scheduling. Lee et al. (2026) ; Potaptchik et al. Therefore, it is common to rely on zero-shot hyperparameter transfer rules to identify optimal hyperparameters when scaling the model size, batch size, and token horizon ( Yang et al., 2022 ; Dey et al., 2026 ; Mlodozeniec et al., 2025 ) . We attempted to leverage Complete(d)P ( Mlodozeniec et al., 2025 ) by performing a hyperparameter sweep on a 400 400 M model; see Section D.3 . Since our architecture includes time-conditioning layers that are not covered by existing transfer theories, we adapted the method by treating these layers as hidden layers. However, our experiments in Section D.4 show that the baseline approach, with neither depth nor width transfer, achieved the best performance. Early work by Dieleman et al. (2022) attempted to learn the embeddings of the discrete data using the reparametrisation trick; Li et al. (2022) explored a similar approach with word embeddings. Later, Stark et al. (2024) designed an interpolation scheme directly on the simplex. Davis et al. (2024) ; Cheng et al. (2024) leveraged Riemannian geometry to alleviate the issues of linear interpolants. Variational Flow Matching ( Eijkelboom et al., 2025 ) shows how to flow from a Gaussian to one-hot encoded data. CFM ( Roos et al., 2026 ) , FMLM ( Lee et al., 2026 ) , and DFM ( Potaptchik et al., 2026b ) adopted this approach, and reached competitive performance with discrete diffusion baselines. Our work builds directly on this line, and demonstrates its scalability to the 1.7 1.7 B parameter regime. Accelerated sampling. Consistency models ( Song et al., 2023 ; Song and Dhariwal, 2023 ) pioneered the idea of mapping any point along a diffusion trajectory to the trajectory’s endpoint, enabling one- or few-step generation. Flow map matching ( Boffi et al., 2025a ; Boffi et al., 2025b ; Geng et al., 2025 ) provides a principled framework for learning such maps via self-distillation of a pretrained flow. CFMs ( Roos et al., 2026 ; Lee et al., 2026 ; Potaptchik et al., 2026b ) port flow map matching to the semi-discrete setting, reducing inference to a single forward pass while retaining the continuous-state benefits. Other related works are discussed in Appendix A . 6 Limitations CFMs require materialising full L × | V | L\times\lvert V\rvert continuous-state trajectory matrices for all steps. At our scale ( L = 2048 L=2048 , | V | ≈ 100 ​ k \lvert V\rvert\approx 100\text{k} ), this is manageable given sufficient hardware ( 256 256 H100s), but the cost grows linearly in context length and vocabulary size. We absorb this bottleneck through compute and efficient cross-entropy implementation ( Wijmans et al., 2025 ) , without solving it. Moreover, CFMs also present challenges in principled hyperparameter transfer. Unlike standard transformers, CFMs condition on continuous times via dedicated layers, which fall outside the parametrisations covered by Complete(d)P ( Mlodozeniec et al., 2025 ) . Our attempts to apply Complete(d)P to this architecture resulted in worse performance than direct tuning at the target scale. Adapting time-conditioned variants of μ \mu P ( Zheng et al., 2025 ) is left for future work. 7 Conclusion We have shown that Categorical Flow Maps scale competitively to the 1.7 1.7 B-parameter regime. After self-distillation, they produce diverse, high-quality text in as few as 4 4 function evaluations while maintaining near-data-level token entropy, pushing the quality vs. throughput Pareto front beyond discrete diffusion baselines. Our semi-discrete ELBO places the model in the same ballpark as other non-autoregressive methods, though a gap remains with approaches trained directly on ELBO maximisation. These results suggest that continuous-state generation is a viable path for discrete data at LLM scale, and that the broader flow map toolbox (guidance, tilting, reward fine-tuning) is now within reach for language modelling.
